name: Quitting smoking / vaping
lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is a lifestyle change that appearance communities associate with healthier-looking, younger-looking skin, brighter teeth, easier breathing and training, and a fresher overall look. The facial pattern seen in many long-term smokers, often called smoker's face, includes a characteristic wrinkle pattern, sagging and a sallow, greyish skin tone; people who stop smoking do so partly to avoid or slow these changes.[1]

The best-known comparison is a 1985 BMJ study by D. Model, which reported the facial features in about 46% of continuing smokers but only about 8% of former smokers with a ten-year smoking history, and in none of the non-smoking controls.[1] Dermatology reviews describe laboratory and epidemiological findings that point the same way: tobacco smoke extract reduces collagen production and raises matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that break down collagen and elastic fibres, and reactive oxygen species appear to be involved.[2][3] A review by Morita suggested that skin ageing may be a motivating argument for appearance-conscious patients to quit.[2]

Research on vaping has concentrated on the lungs and cardiovascular system rather than on facial appearance, although laboratory work on cultured skin cells has begun to look at e-cigarette fluids.[6][10][11][12] On looksmaxxing forums the topic runs in two directions: some members describe nicotine from vapes as an appetite suppressant and leanmaxxing tool, while others describe quitting as part of a routine to improve skin, stamina and general condition. Reported experiences are anecdotal.[13][14][15][16]

chain: Less collagen breakdown and better skin oxygenation
Fewer smoker's-face features, healthier colour and tone
angle.text: Smoking is classed as an extrinsic ager of skin, so stopping removes a recurring source of collagen loss, vessel narrowing and oxidative stress. In the 1985 BMJ comparison, the smoker's-face features were far less common in former smokers than in continuing smokers.[1] People also describe quitting as improving skin colour, breathing and training capacity.[8]

paras: Smoker's face is the name given to a set of changes that many tobacco smokers show: accelerated facial ageing, a pattern of wrinkling, and a dull or yellowish complexion. Wikipedia lists associated changes elsewhere in the body as hair loss, gum disease, tooth decay, tooth staining and a higher skin cancer risk.[1] Smoking is classed as an extrinsic ageing factor, meaning that the ageing is driven by an environmental exposure rather than by time alone.[1]

Proposed mechanisms, as summarised by Wikipedia and by dermatology reviews, include elevated matrix metalloproteinases that degrade collagen, elastin and proteoglycans; narrowing of the small blood vessels so that less oxygen reaches the skin; lower levels of antioxidants such as vitamin C; and a build-up of reactive oxygen species that overwhelms the skin's defences.[1][2] In cultured skin fibroblasts, water-soluble tobacco smoke extract mainly caused oxidative stress and impaired collagen production, and several smoke constituents activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor pathway, which the authors of a 2009 review suggested may contribute to smoke-related ageing.[3]

sections.h: What the research on smoking and appearance shows
paras: The 1985 Model study in the BMJ, titled 'Smoker's face: an underrated clinical sign?', is the comparison most often cited: the facial features were seen in about 46% of continuing smokers and about 8% of former smokers, and not in non-smokers.[1] It is an observational comparison, so it describes association rather than the time course of recovery.

A 2001 study from Japan used silicone replicas of the forearm skin of 63 volunteers and computer imaging to measure surface furrows. Smokers with at least 35 pack-years had greater furrow depth and variability, and fewer furrow lines, than non-smokers, and the replica measurements correlated with clinical wrinkle grading.[4]

A 2009 study in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery examined 186 pairs of identical twins at a festival in Twinsburg, Ohio, using questionnaires and digital photographs rated by a panel. A longer smoking history was associated with looking older, and smoking was associated with more facial wrinkles, alongside other factors such as sun exposure and lack of sunscreen use.[5] Because twins share genes, the design lets differences in habits such as smoking be compared directly.

sections.h: What quitting is reported to change
paras: Reviews describe the skin-ageing effects of smoking as dose-related and linked to ongoing exposure, which is the basis for the argument that stopping removes a recurring source of collagen loss, vessel narrowing and oxidative stress.[2][3] In the Model comparison, the features were far less common in former smokers than in continuing smokers.[1] The available studies do not state how quickly or how completely skin changes recover after stopping.

General health milestones after quitting, as summarised on Wikipedia, include blood pressure and heart rate dropping within about twenty minutes, carbon monoxide levels returning to normal within a few days, improved smell and taste within about two days, better circulation and lung function within about three months, a coronary heart disease risk roughly halved after one to two years, and a lung cancer death risk halved after about ten years.[8] A T Nation member in a long-running quit thread wrote, a week in, that his skin had color and he could breathe more easily.[16]

Weight is a common concern for people who stop. Wikipedia reports an average gain of roughly 4 to 5 kg at twelve months, mostly in the first three months.[8] A 2021 meta-analysis of nine cohort studies by Wang and colleagues found that quitters had a lower cardiovascular risk than continuing smokers whether or not they gained weight, with a pooled relative risk of 0.74 for quitters who gained weight and 0.86 for those who did not.[7]

Vaping is often described by users as a way to stop smoking or to curb appetite. Medical reviews describe it as not free of risk: the 2019 outbreak of e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) led to more than 2,800 hospitalizations in the United States, and a BMJ review noted that the consequences of long-term use are still unknown.[10][11][12] An American Heart Association scientific statement notes that e-cigarettes are regulated as tobacco products and so do not go through the premarket safety studies required of drugs.[12] A cardiology review observed that 'healthier' should not be confused with 'harmless'.[17]

Direct research on vaping and facial skin is limited to laboratory work. A 2021 study of cultured human keratinocytes and a 3D skin model found that e-cigarette refill fluids increased reactive oxygen species and triggered release of the inflammatory markers IL-1 alpha, IL-6 and MMP-9, and the authors concluded that e-cigarette chemicals may cause oxidative damage and inflammation in skin.[6] No study found has measured facial skin changes in people after they stop vaping.

For smoking, Wikipedia summarises nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion and varenicline as first-line medicines, with behavioural support combined with medication raising quit success substantially; unassisted long-term quit rates are reported as around 3 to 6% per attempt, and a 2018 meta-analysis of 61 trials found about 20% of people using drug aids abstinent at one year versus 12% on placebo.[8]

For vaping, randomized trials in young people have tested a text-message cessation program for adolescents, evaluated in a two-group double-blind trial with follow-ups at one and seven months, and varenicline added to brief remote counseling, evaluated over 12 weeks in a three-group trial.[18][19] Both are trials of quitting rates rather than skin outcomes.

On looksmax.org, threads describe nicotine vaping as an appetite suppressant for cutting weight. One poster wrote of eating one meal a day and expecting hollow cheeks; another credited vaping and caffeine with a 40-pound loss, using a candy-flavored vape against sweet cravings and planning to quit after the cut.[13][14] Replies in these threads push the other way, saying vaping made their lungs feel burnt or that they stopped because of concerns about bone growth.[13][15]

Other threads address stopping: one asks whether quitting smoking helps rebuild collagen, and others ask whether vaping stunts height or growth.[20][21] The forum material is anecdotal, and the research on height and growth effects of vaping was not found in the medical reviews on vaping.

Tobacco smoking is described by Wikipedia as a leading cause of preventable death, with the WHO estimating about 8 million deaths a year from tobacco use, and tobacco smoke containing over 7,000 chemicals, 69 of them known carcinogens.[9] Quitting is associated with falling risks over years, including a lung cancer risk that begins to fall soon after stopping and halves after about ten years.[8][9] Nicotine withdrawal and weight changes are common experiences during cessation, and medical support such as that described above is available.

No studies found on quitting vaping for appearance. For smoking, observational studies have compared facial features and skin measurements in smokers, former smokers and non-smokers, including the 1985 BMJ comparison, a 2001 skin-replica study and a 2009 twin study.[1][4][5] Randomized trials of vaping cessation measure quitting rates rather than skin outcomes.[18][19]

timeline.event: D. Model publishes 'Smoker's face: an underrated clinical sign?' in the BMJ, reporting the features in about 46% of continuing smokers and 8% of former smokers.[1]
Yin, Morita and Tsuji report skin-replica measurements in 63 volunteers showing deeper forearm furrows in heavy smokers.[4]
Morita publishes a review in the Journal of Dermatological Science concluding that tobacco smoke causes premature skin ageing.[2]
Twin study of facial ageing in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery links smoking history to looking older and to more wrinkles.[5]
EVALI outbreak in the United States leads to more than 2,800 hospitalizations.[12]
A laboratory study reports oxidative stress and inflammation in cultured human skin cells exposed to e-cigarette fluids.[6]
JAMA publishes a randomized trial of a text-message vaping cessation program for adolescents.[18]
JAMA publishes a randomized trial of varenicline for youth vaping cessation.[19]

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss nicotine in two ways: as a leanmaxxing aid and as something to quit for skin, lungs and stamina.[13][14]

claims.claim: Nicotine vaping suppresses appetite and gives a leaner, hollow-cheeked face
claims.believers: Posters say a vape helped them eat one meal a day or lose around 40 pounds, using a flavored vape against sweet cravings.[13][14]
claims.experts: Reviews describe vaping as linked to lung injury and cardiovascular changes, and say vaping is not without risk.[10][12][17]

claims.claim: Vaping and smoking hurt looks or stunt growth
claims.believers: Members say it makes lungs feel burnt or is bad for bone growth, and some start threads about quitting.[15][20]
claims.experts: The medical reviews found address lung and heart effects of vaping, not growth; a laboratory study reports oxidative stress and inflammation in cultured skin cells exposed to e-cigarette fluids.[6][10][12]

claims.claim: Quitting smoking lets skin rebuild collagen
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether collagen can be rebuilt after quitting.[21]
claims.experts: The smoker's-face comparison found the features far less common in former smokers than current ones; dermatology reviews describe smoke extract reducing collagen production and raising collagen-degrading enzymes. How skin recovers over time is not described in these studies.[1][2][3]

claims.claim: Quitting leaves you fatter, so it costs you looks
claims.believers: People who stop often worry about weight gain, and some forum members use nicotine specifically to stay lean.[13][14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports an average gain of 4 to 5 kg in the first year, and a 2021 meta-analysis found lower cardiovascular risk in quitters whether or not they gained weight.[7][8]

claims.believers: Dermatology-minded posters and quit-thread members describe better colour and breathing after stopping.[16]
claims.experts: The twin study, the skin-replica study and the 1985 BMJ comparison all associate smoking with more wrinkling or older-looking skin.[1][4][5]

card.summary: Quitting smoking or vaping to slow skin aging; smoker's face is documented, quitting's facial reversal is thinly studied.
card.note: Nicotine cessation: seek medical support if needed.

quick.overview:
Smokers show a characteristic aged look: wrinkles and grey, sallow skin. Some people quit hoping to look younger.

Observational data show the features are less common in former smokers, but reversal is not well established.
quick.mechanism: Smoking raises collagen-degrading enzymes, narrows blood vessels and increases oxidative stress.
quick.risks: Smoking carries major documented harms including cancers, heart and lung disease. Quitting is associated with falling lung cancer risk over years.
